done_when: Forge records hold, owner decision, wait and resume times with timestamps, keeps the first start of an item through rewrites and fix-to-task moves, and the How it went record splits start-to-merge into these parts; new and existing repos get it on upgrade

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Not done
Case: normal use - A fix has recorded worker or review time before it is promoted into a story.
The promoted task keeps the fix's start step, but the history reader filters events and timings by the new task key. The old measurements remain under the fix key and disappear from the task's breakdown even when the local logs are available. The rebuild also starts at the task-state addition, after the move; see src/forge/backfill.py:103-111 and src/forge/story.py:1142-1152.
findings.title: Not done: Preserve recorded fix activity when it becomes a task

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Not done
Case: normal use - A human merges a ready pull request several days after Forge closes it.
How it went is last published when the item becomes ready, so its waiting total ends then rather than at the merge. The merged-PR path in src/forge/close.py:186-193 returns without refreshing the record; src/forge/merge.py:179-181 also refreshes before its merge. The board can use GitHub's merge time, but the published How it went record remains a pre-merge snapshot.
findings.title: Not done: Include the final merge wait in How it went

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 2, Harm 4
Raise: Not done
Case: normal use - An earlier Forge release has already published a rebuilt record whose rewritten commit date replaced the saved task start.
The new saved-start search only runs inside rebuild. The upgrade scan skips every pull request that already has a time record, including one with the incorrect start (src/forge/backfill.py:234-237), so its published How it went remains wrong after upgrade. The named upgrade test supplies a pull request without a prior record.
findings.title: Not done: Repair previously published starts on upgrade

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Not done
Case: normal use - An upgraded repository reads a longer item's previously compacted pull-request history, where the earlier release classified uncovered gaps as nothing running.
This change classifies newly derived intervals as unknown, but src/forge/time_records.py:663-669 and 818-835 carry an existing summary's category totals and round text forward unchanged. Its nothing_running total therefore survives, and src/forge/board_app/now.js:86-90 still adds it to time waiting on people. Folded older round text can also retain the old label.
findings.title: Not done: Reclassify gaps in earlier compacted histories

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 1, Harm 3
Raise: Not done
Case: normal use - A worker asks the owner a question and later resumes with the answer.
Forge records the question as a worker question event and the answer as owner wait end (src/forge/worker.py:230-232 and 420-424), but the milestone list omits worker question. How it went shows the wait's end without its start timestamp. It likewise omits a recorded lane left end when a queued run is cancelled.
findings.title: Not done: Show the recorded boundaries of all waits

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Test
Case: normal use - A worked fix is promoted, or an earlier release already published its history before upgrade.
The promoted-fix parameter writes a task state with the desired start and a from_fix field directly; it never runs the fix-to-story move, so it passes even if that move loses the start or recorded activity. The upgrade fixture also starts with no published time record, so it cannot catch the existing-record upgrade failure. The only start assertion rounds the elapsed time to whole days.
findings.title: Gate: Prove promotion and existing published starts

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Test
Case: normal use - A worker waits for an answer, or a ready pull request waits for a human merge.
The named lifecycle proof asserts timestamps for hold, decision and resume only, then ends after close. It would still pass if every wait-start or wait-end milestone were missing, and it never checks the final start-to-merge breakdown. The existing question-wait test checks board intervals but not those timestamps in How it went.
findings.title: Gate: Prove wait timestamps through the final merge

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Test
Case: normal use - A worker repairs a blocked review and calls close again in the same turn.
The named proof writes the expected private event-log records directly, then reads the board. It never runs that worker and both closes, so it still passes if Forge stops producing the events needed to measure or assign the repair. This leaves the named repair behavior without the required command-level proof.
findings.title: Gate: Prove same-turn repairs through a real worker turn

why: Start-to-merge records are unreliable: starts can be rewritten (a task's early commits rewritten to one later time, a fix that became a task keeping the child's start), repairs show zero minutes, and unexplained time is labelled 'nothing running'
